gxy88n: In «la lana con la que tejemos», the words «con la que» have no stress of their own: they are said quickly and joined to the strong syllable of the verb, «con-la-que-te-JE-mos». The same happens with «de quien», «en el que», «a las que». The main stress falls on the antecedent noun and on the verb.
1n6aosp: That is why there is no pause after the preposition. If you say «la lana con… la que tejemos», it sounds as if you are searching for the word. The natural pause, if needed, comes before the preposition or at the end of the relative clause.
1w7kukm: Bear in mind that relative «quien» and «que» have no written accent and are unstressed; the question words «quién» and «qué» do have an accent and are stressed. The audio uses the browser's speech synthesis: it does not certify a regional accent or assess your pronunciation.

28pjkq: Feature published in a travel and culture magazine about a weaving workshop in San Luis. The people and the workshop are fictional.
steawj: Half an hour from the city of San Luis, in an adobe house with a veranda, Elsa Lucero has woven every morning since she was twelve. The loom she works on takes up half the room and creaks every time she passes the shuttle. «My father made it out of carob wood», she says, «and it is better than many new looms I have seen».
1ctk104: Elsa did not study the craft at any school. She learned it from her mother, who in turn had learned it from a neighbour from Renca of whom only one photograph survives today. That is why, when someone asks her about her method, the answer is always the same: «I do it just as I was taught». She warps the threads in the courtyard, dyes the wool with plants from the hills and weaves the way people wove a century ago.
tg7c7i: However, not everything in the workshop is tradition. Her grandson Joaquín, who studied design in Buenos Aires, came back three years ago with an idea that at first seemed to the family riskier than they could afford: selling online. Today the Luceros' ponchos and blankets reach shops in Mendoza, Córdoba and Valencia, and sales have grown much more than anyone expected.
rd1s4t: The change also brought problems nobody had counted on. The first large order, forty blankets for a hotel, took them twice the expected time and they needed more wool than they had bought. «We learned to calculate», Joaquín admits, «and to explain to the customer that a handmade piece is not manufactured as if it were a T-shirt».
shpm80: What has not changed is the relationship with customers. Elsa insists that each buyer choose the colours as they prefer and on sending them photos of the samples before starting. Buyers who find it hard to wait always get the same answer: the wool is dyed according to the weather, and the weather cannot be hurried.
whns89: At the end of the visit, Elsa gives us a table runner with jarilla stripes. She wraps it with enormous care, just as if she were handing us a family heirloom. Perhaps, in a way, it is one.

We learned the craft from our aunt Nélida, a potter with whom we spent every summer of our childhood and from whom we inherited the wood-fired kiln we still use. She used to say that clay teaches more than any book, and over the years we came to agree with her.

We prepare the glazes ourselves, depending on the earth we bring from the river, and that is why no two cups come out the same. When someone commissions a piece, we choose the shape and colour together, and then we make it however the customer prefers, even if their choice sometimes surprises us.
